newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU Parliament warns Brussels over BSE.
newsitem.headline: EU Parliament warns Brussels over BSE.

text.p: The European Parliament's main political groups confirmed on Tuesday that they would threaten to sack the European Commission unless it corrected serious shortcomings over the mad cow crisis.

The leaders of the Socialists, Christian Democrats (EPP) and Greens confirmed their groups would back on Wednesday a joint resolution which calls on the Commission to take "urgent and effective action" to prevent any recurrence of the public health scare caused by the mad cow epidemic.
The resolution differs from a flat-out censure motion due on Thursday that is expected to get little support.
Commission President Jacques Santer was due later on Tuesday to try to persuade the parliament that the measures the Commission planned to take would be sufficient.

Parliament's draft resolution says the Commission must comply with recommendations set out in a scathing report drafted by the parliament's committee of inquiry into the fatal brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

The report attacks the Commission for giving protection of the beef market priority over public health, Britain for failing to enforce eradication measures, and both for negligence and minimising the risks.
"If the recommendations have not been carried out within a reasonable deadline and in any event by November 1997, a motion of censure...will then be tabled," the parliament's draft resolution warns.
But the three groups made it clear it would be left to the parliamentary committees who will monitor the Commission over coming months to decide if sanctions should be imposed.

Reimer Boege, Christian Democrat chairman of the committee of inquiry, said that a petition for conditional censure, signed by over 100 Euro-MPs, was "a clear signal to the Commission that these colleagues are willing to act -- at least in principle".
Lord Plumb, former head of the British Conservatives in the European Parliament and a dairy farmer, warned on Tuesday he would not support either the resolution or the report on BSE.
"Whilst mistakes were made and people have said (the British government) could have done better in the past...I don't think that calls for condemnation," he told a news conference.
